newsitem.title: USA: U.S. still has confidence in Mexican leadership.
newsitem.headline: U.S. still has confidence in Mexican leadership.

text.p: U.S. drug czar Barry McCaffrey said on Thursday the United States had confidence in Mexico's leaders despite the arrest of his Mexican counterpart last week.

"We believe their senior leadership are honest," McCaffrey told a House of Representatives Government Reform subcommittee when asked about the arrest of Mexico's top anti-narcotics official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, on charges that he had ties to a drug kingpin.

President Bill Clinton is supposed to decide by Saturday on whether to grant Mexico and 31 other countries certification as allies in the fight against drug trafficking. Countries that are decertified face possible economic sanctions but Clinton could decertify Mexico while giving it a national interest waiver of sanctions.

McCaffrey would not say what recommendation he would give Clinton about certification of Mexico. "What we're going to do in Mexico is to support this president and his senior officers. I don't think we ought to overreact," he said.

McCaffrey, who had praised Gutierrez as recently as January after meetings with him, called his appointment a tragedy and said "Mexico made a terrible choice." He said Gutierrez had a reputation as an aggressive officer who had made drug arrests.

He said he had not passed on any classified information to Gutierrez at their meetings, but Representative John Mica said he was concerned that other Mexican or U.S. officials had shared information with Gutierrez that could jeopardise the lives of U.S. and Mexican drug agents and informants.

The Florida Republican asked the House Intelligence Committee to investigate whether national security had been compromised. "It is unbelievable to me that the chief U.S. counternarcotics official could not be provided with accurate information relating to the background of General Gutierrez," he said in a letter.

"What concerns me more is that some of U.S. officials may have briefed General Gutierrez or his associates with classified counternarcotics information that could endanger the very lives and security of countless individuals and our entire counternarcotics effort in Mexico," Mica added.
